wall.capable: A tool and practice lay more, and the tool wears. A finished wall holds beasts far better than a fence, keeps most raiders out, and does not rot.
wall.known: Walling is the mason's craft too: building or mending in stone needs it. Where a fence stands the wall is refused. A finished wall wants no yearly mending.

water mill.aware: grinding grain at a mill the river turns
water mill.rough: it needs a water wheel and grain to hand; a failed grinding spoils the grain.
water mill.capable: With the hatches drawn to let fish past, the wheel turns slow and grinds less; a silted wheel or worn stones halve it until seen to.
water mill.known: Those who manage the wheel set its gap: shut, it grinds full but holds running fish below. Flour keeps worse than grain: grind for need.

water wheel.does: build a water wheel and leat: a water mill, where the river turns the millstones and grain is ground to flour in the largest batches
water wheel.aware: a mill wheel turned by the river
water wheel.rough: A carpenter's work, set in a building by water that already has dressed millstones; without the stones, or away from water, it is refused.
water wheel.capable: It wants copper and much timber and stone, and many days' work. The leat silts up within the year: then it grinds half until the leat is cleared.
water wheel.known: Where fish run, shut hatches grind at full but hold a run back below the dam; open, they grind half. Held fish are easier taken by hand.

weed.does: weed a growing crop: a cleaner crop bears more when reaped, up to as clean as weeding makes it
weed.aware: pulling weeds so a crop bears more
weed.rough: Done on a growing crop; it needs no tool. Weeding a ripe crop does it no good, and the day is wasted.
weed.capable: Practice weeds more ground each go. Each weeding gains less than the last, and a large crop takes many goes to come clean.
weed.known: Past clean it gains nothing: stop and spend the day elsewhere. A crop withered by blight is refused; a strip beside the main crop is never weeded.

weir.does: build a fish weir across a river with a crew: stakes and wattle that turn the fish runs into wicker traps in its gap, which fill by night
weir.aware: stakes across a river that trap fish as they run
weir.rough: Crew work across a river: name who builds it with you. One weir to a place; its first section is wattle unless you say timber.
weir.capable: Lift the catch often: full traps take no more. Shut, its gap takes the runs; open, very little. Floods and ice wear it, a shut gap in high water most.
weir.known: Add sections and stone footings to take more and wear less; timber outlasts wattle. Mend it a section at a time. Taking from another crew's weir is theft, and seen.

wicker trap.does: make a wicker trap: set in the water, it fishes by night until you take it up; it wears with the nights and is mended
wicker trap.aware: a basket trap of withies for eels and fish
wicker trap.rough: woven of withies; a failed try wastes them. A trap is set in water, never on dry land.
wicker trap.capable: Each night set wears it; worn through, it comes home broken and wants mending, a little withy each. It rots slowly, faster in water.
wicker trap.known: Make several: one setting lays a few traps together, and spares replace those a spate tears away.

wooden plough.does: make a wooden plough: drawn by a yoked pair of oxen in harness, it breaks a field far faster than a hoe; it wears out with the ground it breaks
wooden plough.aware: a wooden plough, drawn by a pair of oxen
wooden plough.rough: a long piece of work; a failed try spoils the timber and copper. Without oxen and harness to draw it, it does nothing.
wooden plough.capable: It is never mended: every plot ploughed wears it until it is done. Ploughing over a standing crop turns it under.
wooden plough.known: Two oxen you may use, two harnesses and the plough must all be to hand; worked by others' oxen, their holders are told.

woodshed.does: build a woodshed: a lean-to against a building where a great stack of timber, firewood and charcoal is kept off the house's floor
woodshed.aware: a lean-to for stacking fuel and timber
woodshed.rough: Put against a finished building, taking ground beside it, not floor; with no free building ground there it is refused.
woodshed.capable: It holds only timber, firewood and charcoal. It is part of the house's store, so the hearth burns from it first.
woodshed.known: Without one, a winter's fuel crowds the floor and spills outside the door, where it still burns but lies open to anyone.
